case_name: Young and Young v. McLellan et al
text:
IN THE SUPREME
COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Young and Young v. McLellan et al,

2004 BCSC 995

Date: 20040726

Docket:
04 0098

Registry: Victoria

Between:

Eric Young and Marlene Young

Plaintiffs

And

Anne McLellan and Her Majesty the
Queen in Right of Canada

Defendants

Before: The Honourable Mr. Justice Vickers

(In
Chambers)

Reasons for Judgment

Eric Young and Marlene Young:

In
Person

Counsel for the Defendants:

K.
Manning

Date and Place of Trial/Hearing:

July
15, 2004

Victoria,
B.C.

[
1
]

This is a motion that the writ of summons and
statement of claim be struck for failure to disclose a reasonable cause of
action pursuant to Rule 19(24) and on the grounds that they are an abuse of the
Court’s process or, in the alternative, for an order that:

a)   The Attorney General of Canada be substituted as defendant
for Her Majesty the Queen in Right of Canada;

b)   The defendant Anne McLellan be struck as a party to this
action;

c)   The plaintiffs be required to provide further particulars
of any alleged misrepresentations;

d)   The plaintiffs be required to provide further particulars
of specifically which allegedly defamatory statements made by the defendants
are false;

e)   The defendants be given an extension of time of 30 days to
file and serve their Statements of Defence after the date of the resulting
order.

[
2
]

It is convenient to set out in full, the
plaintiffs’ statement of claim, as follows:

The Plaintiffs

1.   The
Plaintiffs are husband and wife and reside at 3945 Morgan St. Victoria, BC, V8X
1Z8.

2.   Before
becoming ill Plaintiff Eric Young was an assistant professor in Computer
Engineering and Plaintiff Marlene Young was a visual artist.

3.   Plaintiff
Eric Young was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in February 1996 after
experiencing left side paralysis.

4.   Plaintiff
Eric Young experiences many of the horrible, often invisible, symptoms of this
life threatening chronic progressive incurable brain disease, including but not
limited to, weakness, fatigue, lack of concentration, anorexia, vision loss,
balance problems, spasticity, pain, seizures.

5.   Plaintiff
Eric Young successfully controls his symptoms and the progression of multiple
sclerosis using cannabis sativa, without side effects, replacing a cocktail of
far less effective toxic pharmaceutical drugs.

6.   On June 15,
1999, Plaintiff Eric Young's general practitioner prescribed cannabis to treat
his multiple sclerosis.

The Defendants

7.   Defendant
Anne McLellan was educated as a lawyer and served as the Minister of Health
from January 2002 to December 2003, and the Minister of Justice and Attorney
General of Canada from June 1997 to January 2002.

8.   Her Majesty
the Queen in Right of Canada (the Crown) is responsible for the conduct of
officers, employees, and agents of Health Canada which includes the Office of
the Director General of the Drug Strategy and Controlled Substances Programme
and the Office of Cannabis Medical Access.

9.   Health
Canada's "mission and vision" is:

"Health Canada is the federal
department responsible for helping the people of Canada maintain and improve
their health.

Health Canada strives to improve the
health of all Canada's people, while respecting individual choices and
circumstances, and therefore seeks to put Canada among the countries with the
healthiest people in the world."

Legal context

10.  On September
1, 1999, Plaintiff Eric Young applied for a personal use exemption pursuant to

s. 56
of the
Controlled Drugs and Substances Act
, S.C. 1996, c. 19,
(CDSA), to possess and cultivate cannabis for medical purpose.

11.  A s. 56
personal use exemption requires the support of a general practitioner.

12.  On March 10,
2000, Plaintiff Eric Young was exempted from the
CDSA
to possess and cultivate
cannabis for his medical purpose.

13.  On December
12, 2001, Plaintiff Marlene Young was exempted from the
CDSA
to possess and
cultivate cannabis for her husband's medical purpose.

14.  There are
fiduciary relationships between each Defendant and the Plaintiffs because of
the elements of power, discretion, and influence on the part of the Defendants,
the fiduciary, and reliance, vulnerability, trust, and confidence on the part
of the Plaintiffs, the beneficiary.

15.  A s. 56
personal use exemption is valid for a specified period of time, with six months
renewals and most recently annual renewals.

16.  Upon expiry
of a personal use exemption, the patient is required to reapply, by
resubmitting information, to maintain access to his/her medicine.

17.
S. 56
of the

CDSA
gives sole discretion to the Minister of Health to grant exemptions from
the CDSA.

18.  On July 31,
2000, the Ontario Court of Appeal held in R. v. Parker,
2000 CanLII 5762 (ON CA)
, 146 C.C.C. (3d) 193,
that provisions of the
CDSA
were unconstitutional, due to the unfettered
discretion given to the Health Minister by
s. 56
with respect to personal use
exemptions for medicinal cannabis, and suspended the invalidity for one year.

19.  On July 30,
2001, the
Marihuana Medical Access Regulations
, SOR 2001-227, (MMAR),
came into force legitimizing the use of cannabis for medicinal purposes.

20.  The
MMAR

allowed for a six month extension of a valid s. 56 personal use exemption after
which time the patient must qualify under a new stricter rule which requires a
specialist, not a general practitioner as for a s. 56 personal use exemption,
to sign the application form for a category two patient like Plaintiff Eric
Young.

21.  Despite
numerous attempts and the support of his general practitioner, Plaintiff Eric
Young, like others, has been unable to find a specialist that will sign the
form required to qualify for the
MMAR
.

22.  On June 24,
2002, Plaintiff Eric Young launched a challenge, yet to be answered,
questioning the constitutionality of the
MMAR
, SCBC Victoria Registry no. 02
3057.

23.  On October 7,
2003, the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that the
MMAR
were not
constitutional and struck them down in part.

24.  The granting
of a s. 56 exemption remains at the sole discretion of the Minister of Health.

Defendants'
conduct

25.  The renewals
of the Plaintiffs' exemptions have been issued either on, close to, or after
the expiry date.

26.  The initial
exemption of Plaintiff Marlene Young and the Plaintiffs' renewals have often
contained material errors, e.g. incorrect name or dosage.

27.  On February
19, 2002, after being unable to reach the Office of Cannabis Medical Access
(OCMA), the Plaintiffs called the Office of the Director General of the Drug
Strategy and Controlled Substances Programme, Dr. Gomber, as their exemptions
were expiring March 11, 2002, and Plaintiff Eric Young could not find a
specialist to sign the required form.

28.  Plaintiff
Eric Young spoke with Roxanne Vezina, employee of Dr. Gomber's office,
inquiring about the procedure to follow for a holder of a s. 56 personal use
exemption if they cannot find a specialist.

29.  Afterwards
Ms. Vezina spoke with Carol Langlois, an employee of Health Canada, and wrote
him an email containing false and defamatory statements:

"Subject:  Phone message-Eric Young

Mr. Eric Young
called to speak to the EA of the DG – Jody Gomber on February 19th, 2002 at
around 11 AM.

Cindy was not at her
desk therefore I answered her phone.  A gentleman mentioned that he would like
the DG to make it so that his wife and himself are exempt for life under
Section 45.  OR if not for just a year.

He is infuriated
that no doctors will sign his application under MMAR and that we are asking him
to re-apply.

The phone call
became derogatory (profanity) towards Cheryle Anderson who he claims has been
rude and of no use.  He mentioned repeadedly [sic] that Health Canada only
deserves to see him die and that he would fly down to Parliament Hill or Ottawa
and starve himself to die.  He was very rude and aggitated [sic].  After 1 1/2
hour of constant complaining he said the only way to make Health Canada stand
up and take notice is to bomb OCMA and all of HC.  I mentioned this to Carol Langlois
who will discuss it with all concerning [sic] parties.  At this point Mr. Young
will only speak to Cindy Cripps-Prawak to get a solution.  He would like her to
call him back "this (profanity) year".

Hope this summary is
helpful, please call on me if you have any questions.

Roxane J. Vézina

946-1470"

30.  Based on this
email, Ray Sabourin, of the Safety, Emergency and Security Management Division
with Health Canada, called the RCMP and the Saanich Police and later sent a fax
to the Saanich Police at 17:49 pm (EST) alleging that Plaintiff Eric Young made
a bomb threat.

31.  In addition,
Mr. Sabourin disclosed private medical information to the RCMP and the Saanich
Police, without consent, about Plaintiff Eric Young's exemption, said information
being irrelevant to the alleged purpose of the call.

32.  On April 24,
2002, Lloyd Duhaime, counsel for the Plaintiffs at the time, wrote to Defendant
Anne McLellan requesting an apology but Defendant Anne McLellan ignored the
request or refused to apologize and retract the accusation.

33.  On many
occasions Defendant Anne McLellan spoke negatively about cannabis as medicine,
including but not limited to, on August 19, 2002, when Defendant Anne McLellan
answered a question while giving a speech at the annual meeting of the Canadian
Medical Association and misrepresented the medicinal use of cannabis.

34.  On August 27,
2002, the Plaintiffs were told by Valerie Lasher, Acting Director of the OCMA,
that Defendant Anne McLellan denied to extend their exemptions, which were due
to expire on September 11, 2002, after, at the request of Glen Rosenfeld,
Health Canada counsel, Plaintiff Eric Young wrote to Defendant Anne McLellan,
the Health Minister, and to the Deputy Health Minister's Office, providing
documentation of support from his general practitioner.

35.  Plaintiff
Eric Young initiated a motion in the Supreme Court of British Columbia, within
his constitutional challenge, SCBC Victoria Registry no. 02 3057, seeking
interim constitutional exemptions.

36.  On September
5, 2002, exemptions were issued to the Plaintiffs a day before the motion
seeking interim constitutional exemptions was to be heard.

37.  On August 21,
2003, after the OCMA refused to confirm that the Plaintiffs' exemptions would
be extended, the Plaintiffs initiated another interim application to maintain
their exemptions which were due to expire on September 11, 2003.

38.  On August 28,
2003, Defendant Anne McLellan "renewed" the Plaintiffs' exemption
and, without giving notice, withdrew Plaintiff Eric Young's exemption for
cultivating thereby exposing him to criminal prosecution by forcing him to live
without protection.

39.  Later that
day, after the Plaintiffs refused to adjourn the motion, Defendant Anne
McLellan restored Plaintiff Eric Young's exemption for cultivating.

40.  On or before
September 5, 2003, employees of Health Canada electronically reproduced
photographs of the Plaintiffs against the Plaintiffs' request that the
photographs not be reproduced.

41.  The
Plaintiffs have only managed to maintain their exemptions through legal
actions.

42.  Defendant
Anne McLellan acted outside her jurisdiction when she denied in whole or in
part to extend the Plaintiff's exemptions.

43.  Defendant
Anne McLellan deliberately denied to extend in whole or in part the Plaintiffs'
exemptions.

44.  Defendant
Anne McLellan was aware that she was acting outside her jurisdiction and that
this was likely to harm Plaintiff Eric Young by withdrawing his successful
palliative care and the ensuing emotional stress and mental anxiety to the
Plaintiffs.

Causes of action

45.  On February
19, 2002, Ms. Vezina and Mr. Sabourin, employees of Health Canada, made oral
and written defamatory statements about Plaintiff Eric Young to other Health
Canada employees, the RCMP, and the Saanich Police.

46.  On February
19, 2002, Mr. Sabourin invaded the Plaintiffs' privacy rights when he
disclosed, without consent, medical information irrelevant to the alleged
purpose of the call to the RCMP and the Saanich Police.

47.  Defendant
Anne McLellan committed misfeasance of office, on many occasions, when she,
with the intent to harm the Plaintiffs, intentionally committed an illegal act,
that is the refusal to extend in whole or in part the Plaintiffs' exemptions.

48.  The conduct
of employees of Health Canada and Defendant Anne McLellan at the time when the
Plaintiffs' exemptions were up for renewal was intended to harm the Plaintiff
by inflicting nervous shock.

49.  The conduct
of employees of Health Canada and Defendant Anne McLellan at the time when the
Plaintiffs' exemptions were up for renewal was in breach of their fiduciary
duty.

50.  Defendant
Anne McLellan breached her fiduciary duty by misrepresenting the medicinal use
of cannabis.

Damages

51.  The conduct
of Defendant Anne McLellan and employees of Health Canada over a period of more
than 4 years, as set out above, has caused severe emotional stress and mental
anxiety to both Plaintiffs resulting in bouts of depression to the point of
suicidal thoughts.

52.  The Plaintiffs
have incurred financial losses to maintain their exemptions through legal
actions.

53.  As a
consequence of the written and oral defamatory statements of Mr. Sabourin, the
RCMP and the Saanich Police Department databases contain false information
about Plaintiff Eric Young with respect to February 19, 2002.

54.  The
Plaintiffs have suffered loss of dignity and a complete loss of trust in
government.

Relief

The Plaintiffs claim as follows:

(a)

compensatory
damages against both Defendants for severe psychological harm from their
conduct, as set out above:

$10,000 for pain and suffering;

$20,000
for emotional stress and mental anxiety;

$40,000
for loss of enjoyment of life; and general damages;

(b)

with
aggravated and punitive damages against the Crown:

$10,000
for invasion of privacy;

$5,000,000
for defamation; and

$10,000,000
for breach of fiduciary duty;

(c)

aggravated
and punitive damages against Defendant Anne McLellan:

$500,000
for misfeasance of office; and

$1,000,000
for breach of fiduciary duty;

(d)

Costs

Place of the
trial:  Victoria Courthouse, 850 Burdett, Victoria, British Columbia.

[
3
]

Counsel for the defendants sought particulars on
February 5, 2004, as follows:

1.

Paragraph
29

a.

With
respect to the allegation in paragraph 29 of the Statement of Claim that the
email contained "false and defamatory statements", please provide
particulars to identify which statements are alleged to be false and
defamatory.

2.

Paragraph
33

a.

With
respect to the allegation in paragraph 33 of the Statement of Claim that the
Defendant Anne McLellan "misrepresented the medicinal use of
cannabis", please provide particulars to identify:

i.

what
representation was made;

ii.

to
whom the representation was made;

iii.

where
the representation was made;

iv.

the
particulars of the precise nature and extent of the untruth.

b.

Please
also provide the same particulars in respect of each of the "many
occasions" that you allege misrepresentations were made by the Defendant
Anne McLellan in paragraph 33;

c.

Please
also provide particulars with respect to the specific representation or
representations relied upon by each Plaintiff including:

i.

which
Plaintiff relied on which representation or representations by the Defendant
Anne McLellan;

ii.

when
each Plaintiff relied on that, or those, representations;

iii.

the
manner in which each Plaintiff relied on that, or those, representations; and

iv.

what
was the impact on each Plaintiff as a result of relying on each
representation.

[
4
]

In response, the defendants declined to provide
particulars and said that all statements in the allegedly defamatory email
pleaded in paragraph 29 of the statement of claim were false.

[
5
]

On June 25, 2002 the plaintiff Eric Young filed
a petition seeking a declaration that the petitioner’s rights as set out in
s.
7
,
12
or
15
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
have
been infringed.  On May 15, 2003 an amended petition was filed.  This amended
document added Marlene Young as a petitioner.  In addition to the relief sought
in the original petition, the petitions sought an order that Cannabis Sativa
and its derivatives be removed from the
Controlled Drugs and Substances
Act
(
CDSA
), or in the alternative, the
Marihuana Medical
Access Regulations
(MMAR) be struck down, or in the alternative, that the petitioners
be granted constitutional exemptions.  The petitioners also seek a mandatory
injunction that Health Canada undertake a public education campaign with
complete and accurate information about Cannabis Sativa as medicine.  The
petitioners also seek damages.

[
6
]

Many of the matters pleaded in the amended
petition are found in the statement of claim.  The petition sets out in
paragraph 57 and 58 that the respondent Canada made a false allegation of a
bomb threat and without the consent of the petitioner, disclosed private
medical information.

[
7
]

The petitioners now advise that they intend to
discontinue the petition proceedings and to amend the statement of claim in
this action to raise the constitutional issues.  The reason for not filing a notice
of discontinuance was because they are about to apply for another annual
extension of their personal exemption to possess and cultivate cannabis for
medical purposes.  While I am unable to understand the explanation, they are of
the view that discontinuance of the petition proceedings would, in some way,
imperil their application to grant the exemption for another year.

[
8
]

A similar situation, involving a duplication of
proceedings arose in
Great Pacific Contracting Ltd. v. Harwyn Properties
Ltd.

(1981),
1981 CanLII 734 (BC SC)
, 29 B.C.L.R. 145 (S.C.).  Spencer L.J.S.C. said the
following:

¶10  The same
relief already having been sought in an extant proceeding, it was in my opinion
vexatious and an abuse of the process of the Court to seek that relief by a
separate action.  See
Paterson v. Jaikumar
(1979), 10
B.C.L.R. P-48 and
Earl Poulett v. Viscount Hill
,
[1893] 1 Ch.
277
.  Those cases go so far as saying that where the same relief can
be obtained in the first action the plaintiffs are not entitled to bring a
second action for it while the first is still pending.  They appear
to extend to cases where the same relief has not actually been claimed but can
be claimed.  As I have pointed out in the case at Bar the same relief
actually is claimed.

...

¶
12  I am satisfied that this is a clear case where the same relief
is sought in two separate proceedings.  Accordingly the last of the two, that
is the writ and statement of claim must be struck out.  An order will
go accordingly with costs to the defendants.

[
9
]

The plaintiffs are unrepresented and while the
rules cannot be changed for them, it is a factor I have borne in mind in this
matter.  I am not prepared to strike out the writ of summons in this action at
this time.  I am, however, going to make an order that these proceedings be stayed
until such time as the claim for damages in the petition proceedings remains
alive.  When the claim for damages is withdrawn or the petition discontinued
these proceedings may continue, subject to the decision that follows.

[
10
]

Not without difficulty, I have concluded that the statement of claim
attempts to plead the following causes of action.

a)   Breach of fiduciary duty:  paragraphs
14, 49 and 50;

b)   Defamation:  paragraphs 29, 32,
45 and 53;

c)   Invasion of privacy:
paragraph 46;

d)   Abuse of public office: paragraphs 42, 43, 44 and 47;

e)   Infliction of nervous shock:
paragraph 48.

[
11
]

I do not see a claim for misrepresentation in the statement of claim.
The plaintiffs make reference to misrepresentations by Minister McLellan
concerning the medical use of cannabis, but this is more in the nature of
pleading evidence.  There is no plea to the effect that they relied on the
representations of the Minister to their detriment.

[
12
]

The parties to an action must frame their pleadings with certainty
and clarity:
Yewdale v. Insurance Corp. of B.C. et al.
,

[1994]
B.C.J. No. 1892 (S.C.) (QL)
;
Homalco Indian Band v British Columbia

(1998),

1998 CanLII 6658 (BC SC)
, 25 C.P.C. (4th) 107 (B.C.S.C.).  On a motion to strike the pleading, pursuant
to Rule 19(24) the test is whether or not it is plain and obvious that the
action is bound to fail:
Hunt v. Carey
,

1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R.
959.  If there are any doubts they should be resolved in allowing the pleading
to stand:
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish
Congress

(1999), 36 C.P.C. (3d) 112 (B.C.S.C.)
.

[
13
]

In
Guerin v. Canada
,
1984 CanLII 25 (SCC)
, [1984] 2 S.C.R. 335 Dickson J.
said at page 385:

It should be noted
that fiduciary duties generally arise only with regard to obligations
originating in a private law context. Public law duties, the performance of
which requires the exercise of discretion, do not typically give rise to a
fiduciary relationship. As the "political trust" cases indicate, the
Crown is not normally viewed as a fiduciary in the exercise of its legislative
or administrative function.

[
14
]

The exemption provision in s. 56 of the
Controlled Drug and
Substances Act
,

S.C. 1996 c. 19
, reads:

The Minister
may, on such terms and conditions as the Minister deems necessary, exempt any
person or class of persons or any controlled substance or precursor or any
class thereof from the application of all or any of the provisions of this Act
or the regulations if, in the opinion of the Minister, the exemption is
necessary for a medical or scientific purpose or is otherwise in the public
interest.

[
15
]

I conclude that this section requires the Minister to exercise an
administrative function, in the public interest.  It does not give rise to a
fiduciary obligation to those persons in receipt of a s. 56 exemption.

[
16
]

In
Rogers v. Faught

(2001), 5 C.C.L.T. (3d) 109 (Ont.
Sup. Ct.)
, Cameron J. said at para. 62:

Fiduciary
duties generally arise only with regard to obligations originating in a private
law context.  Public law duties, the performance of which requires the exercise
of discretion, do not typically give rise to a fiduciary relationship:
Guerin
v. Canada
(1984),
1984 CanLII 25 (SCC)
, 13 D.L.R. (4th) 321 (S.C.C.) at p. 342;
Farm
Credit Corp. v. Pipe
(1993),
1993 CanLII 8588 (ON CA)
, 16 O.R. (3d) 49 (C.A.) at p. 60-61.  The
obligations owed by the Colleges to the public and their members are
inconsistent with a fiduciary relationship or obligation to a patient or client
of a member because the interests of the public, a member and a member of the
public are bound to conflict.  The primary obligation is to the public.

[
17
]

The plaintiffs, in the course of argument, alleged malice in the
actions of McLellan.  Malice is not pleaded.  Even if it was it would not
change the fact that no fiduciary duty arises in the administration of the
duties imposed by s. 56.

[
18
]

For these reasons the plea of breach of fiduciary duty cannot
succeed.  Accordingly paragraphs 14, 49 and 50 of the statement of claim are
struck.

[
19
]

Paragraph 29 reproduces an email transmission that the plaintiffs
allege is defamatory.  They have declined to provide particulars and have said
the entire transmission is false.  Mr. Young conceded in the course of argument
that the entire transmission is not false.  I decline to strike this plea of
defamation.  There will be an order that the defendants provide particulars as
demanded by the defendants.

[
20
]

The plaintiffs have pleaded invasion of privacy arising out of the
transmission of certain medical information to the Saanich police following an
alleged bomb threat by the plaintiff, Eric Young.

[
21
]

The relevant provisions of the
Privacy Act
, R.S.B.C.
1996, c. 373 read as follows:

1

(1)

It
is a tort, actionable without proof of damage, for a person, wilfully and
without a claim of right, to violate the privacy of another.

(2)

The
nature and degree of privacy to which a person is entitled in a situation or
in relation to a matter is that which is reasonable in the circumstances,
giving due regard to the lawful interests of others.

...

2

(2)

An
act or conduct is not a violation of privacy if any of the following applies:

...

(b)

the
act or conduct was incidental to the exercise of a lawful right of defence of
person or property;

...

[
22
]

Section 74
of the
Privacy Act
, R.S.C. 1985, c. P-21,
reads:

Notwithstanding
any other Act of Parliament, no civil or criminal proceedings lie against the
head of any government institution, or against any person acting on behalf or
under the direction of the head of a government institution, and no proceedings
lie against the Crown or any government institution, for the disclosure in good
faith of any personal information pursuant to this Act, for any consequences
that flow from that disclosure, or for the failure to give any notice required
under this Act if reasonable care is taken to give the required notice.

[
23
]

The pleading of invasion of privacy is not properly framed because
it fails to allege that the violation was “wilfully and without a claim of
right.”  The pleading will have to be amended to make this allegation and state
clearly the material facts relied upon by the plaintiffs to support this plea.
The defendants are entitled to know the private information that was allegedly
transmitted to the police.  S. 2(2) of the British Columbia legislation raises
a defence to be pleaded in the statement of defence.  As well
s. 74
of the
federal

Privacy Act
is a defence based on a good faith transmission of
information.  I am not prepared at this stage to strike this pleading,
preferring to give the plaintiffs the opportunity to make a proper pleading and
provide sufficient particularity in that pleading.

[
24
]

In
Powder Mountain Resorts Ltd. v. British Columbia
,
2001
BCCA 619
, Newbury J.A. said for the majority at paragraph 7 and 8:

Absent some
ruling to the contrary by Supreme Court of Canada, it may, I think, now be
accepted that the tort of abuse of public office will be made out in Canada
where a public official is shown either to have exercised power for the
specific purpose of injuring the plaintiff (i.e., to have acted in "bad
faith in the sense of the exercise of public power for an improper or ulterior
motive") or to have acted "unlawfully with a mind of reckless
indifference to the illegality of his act" and to the probability of
injury to the plaintiff.  (See Lord Steyn in
Three Rivers
, at
8.)  Thus there remains what in theory at least is a clear line between this tort
on the one hand, and what on the other hand may be called negligent excess of
power - i.e., an act committed without knowledge of (or subjective recklessness
as to) its unlawfulness and the probable consequences for the plaintiff.  The
actionability of such conduct, based on "recklessness . . . used in an
objective sense" was rejected by their Lordships in
Three Rivers

(see Lord Steyn at 9-10; Lord Hutton at 37-39; Lord Hobhouse at 44; and Lord
Millett at 49), and has been rejected as well by the High Court of Australia
(see
Northern Territory of Australia v. Mengel

(1995) 185 C.L.R.
307
), and the Court of Appeal of New Zealand (see
Garrett v. Attorney
General
[1997] 2 N.Z.L.R. 332). Perhaps the opinion of Lord Millett in
Three
Rivers
sums up most succinctly the elements of the two branches of the
tort:

. . . If the
plaintiff can establish the official's subjective intention to exercise the
power of his office in order to cause him injury, he does not need to
establish that the official exceeded the terms of the powers conferred upon
him.  If, on the other hand, the plaintiff can establish that the official
appreciated that he was acting in excess of the powers conferred upon him and
that his conduct would cause injury to the plaintiff, the inference that he
acted dishonestly or for an improper purpose will be exceedingly difficult
and usually impossible to rebut.  Moreover . . ., the consequences of his
actions will usually be obvious enough to the official concerned, who can
then be taken to have intended the damage he caused.  I also agree . . . that
intention includes subjective recklessness, that is to say . . . 'a conscious
disregard for the interests of those who will be affected by' the exercise of
the power. [at 49]

Because abuse of public office
remains an intentional tort requiring proof of bad faith, it will in the minds
of most observers carry the 'stench of dishonesty'. This court has suggested
that where bad faith on the part of a public official is alleged, clear proof
commensurate with the seriousness of the wrong should be provided: see
MacMillan
Bloedel Ltd. v. Galiano Island Trust Committee
(1995)
1995 CanLII 4585 (BC CA)
, 10 B.C.L.R. (3d)
121 per Finch J.A. (as he then was) at 181-2. (Lve. to app. to S.C.C. dism'd.,
[1995] S.C.C.A. No. 439). In
First National Properties Ltd. v. McMinn

(2001)
2001 BCCA 305 (CanLII)
, 198 D.L.R. (4th) 443, we also stated that courts should be cautious in
dealing with the tort because it is an exception to the normal disinterest of
the civil law in the motive underlying conduct, as opposed to the conduct
itself:  see
Bradford Corp. v. Pickles

[1895] A.C. 587 (H.L.)
.
(The criminal law distinguishes between "motive" and
"intention" but that distinction seems inoperative in the present
context.)  Motive is of course notoriously difficult to discern, and one may
act for more than one motive.

[
25
]

Thus this is an intentional tort, requiring proof of bad faith.  In
paragraph 47 of the statement of claim, the plaintiffs allege that the
defendant McLellan “committed misfeasance of office when she, on many
occasions, with the intent to harm the plaintiffs, intentionally committed an
illegal act, that is the refusal to extend in whole of in part the Plaintiffs’
exemptions.”

[
26
]

I note that a refusal to extend an exemption is not an illegal act
but an act contemplated by the discretion implicit in s. 56.  It is noteworthy
as well to record that at all material times the plaintiffs have been the
recipient of s. 56 exemptions and are currently the holders of such an
exemption.

[
27
]

No material facts are pleaded to support the plea of abuse of office
and accordingly the plea cannot stand.  Paragraphs 42, 43, 44 and 47 are struck
from the statement of claim.

[
28
]

The final tort alleged is infliction of nervous shock.  As I read
the statement of claim and from the arguments made by Eric Young, the
plaintiffs seem to be saying they sustained nervous shock on two occasions.
The first arose when the police arrived and accused Eric Young, falsely he
says, of making a bomb threat.  This is tied directly to the defamation plea.
The second occasion of nervous shock came with an alleged delay in renewing the
s. 56 exemption.  In that regard the pleadings seem to say that the extension
of the exemption was made about 2 weeks before expiry.  As this is a
discretionary decision I failed to see what duty was owed the plaintiffs to
advise them of their extension any earlier than they did.

[
29
]

In
Rhodes Estate v. C.N.R.
(1990),
1990 CanLII 5401 (BC CA)
, 50 B.C.L.R. (2d)
273 (C.A.), Taylor J.A. points out that this claim is founded in negligence.
It involves an act where it is foreseeable that it would cause mental anguish
or nervous shock.  Wallace J.A. at page 291 said:

Nervous shock
cases, unaccompanied by physical injury, differ significantly from the
traditional case of tortuous conduct inflicting direct physical injury and they
necessitate a different approach in fixing liability.  The difference arises
from the fact that generally the plaintiff's psychiatric injury is alleged to
have been caused by observing, experiencing, or being informed of the injury or
death to a third party (usually a close relative).  In this sense, the injury
is the indirect result of a direct physical injury to a third party. When one
appreciates that grief, sorrow or reactive depression are not compensable, the
problems of determining foreseeability and causation of such psychiatric
illness are clearly apparent.  Accordingly, to resolve the issues of
foreseeability and causation, some factors beyond the psychiatric illness
sustained by the plaintiff and the foreseeability of injury must be established.

[
30
]

In my view, the pleadings do not disclose any tortious conduct of
which it could be said that nervous shock, or a psychological or psychiatric
condition was a foreseeable result.  There will be an order striking paragraph
48 of the statement of claim.

[
31
]

Ann McLellan is not properly a party in these proceedings.  All of
her actions were in a representative capacity.  There are no allegations in the
statement of claim that she did any of the matters alleged in a personal
capacity:
Cairns v. Farm Credit Corp.

(1991),
1991 CanLII 13600 (FC)
, 49 F.T.R. 308;
Air
India Flight 182 Disaster Claimants v. Air India

(1987),
1987 CanLII 4125 (ON SC)
, 44 D.L.R. (4
th
)
317 (Ont. H.C).  There will be an order striking Anne McLellan as a defendant
in these proceedings.

[
32
]

Her Majesty the Queen in Right of Canada is not properly named as a
defendant.  The
Crown Liability and Proceedings Act
,
R.S.C. 1985,
c. C-50, s. 23 reads:

(1)  Proceedings
against the Crown may be taken in the name of the Attorney General of Canada
or, in the case of an agency of the Crown against which proceedings are by an
Act of Parliament authorized to be taken in the name of the agency, in the name
of that agency.

(2)  Where
proceedings are taken against the Crown, the document originating the
proceedings shall be served on the Crown by serving it on the Deputy Attorney
General of Canada or the chief executive officer of the agency in whose name
the proceedings are taken, as the case may be.

[
33
]

I appreciate the use of the word “may” in that provision. In that
regard, I agree with the conclusions reached by Sulyma J., in
Dix v.
Canada
,

2001 ABQB 256
.  There will be an order striking the
defendant Her Majesty the Queen in Right of Canada and substituting therefore,
The Attorney General of Canada, thus amending the style of cause to read
Eric
Young and Marlene Young v. The Attorney General of Canada
.

[
34
]

In summary, I make the following orders:

1.   That these proceedings be stayed as long as the claim for
damages in the petition proceedings remains alive.  When the claim for damages
is withdrawn or the petition discontinued these proceedings may continue,
taking into account the orders that follow;

2.   Paragraphs 14, 49 and 50 of the statement of claim are
struck;

3.   That the defendants provide particulars of paragraph 29 of
the statement of claim as demanded by the defendants;

4.   The pleading alleging an invasion of privacy will be
amended to plead the statutory elements and state clearly the material facts
relied upon by the plaintiffs to support this plea;

5.   Paragraphs 42, 43, 44 and 47 are struck from the statement
of claim;

6.   Paragraph 48 of the statement of claim is struck;

7.   Anne McLellan is struck as a named defendant in these
proceedings; and,

8.   The Attorney General of Canada is substituted as a
defendant in the place of Her Majesty the Queen in Right of Canada.

[
35
]

In addition, there will be an order that the defendant have a period
of 30 days from receipt of the amended statement of claim and particulars, to
file the statement of defence.

[
36
]

The defendant is entitled to recover the costs of this motion, in
the cause.

[
37
]

Finally, I want to recommend that this case have the benefit of a
case management judge.  When the pleadings are closed this request may be made
in the usual manner.

“D.H. Vickers, J.”
